newsitem.title: USA: UAW, Ford suspend labor talks until Monday.
newsitem.headline: UAW, Ford suspend labor talks until Monday.

text.p: Bleary-eyed negotiators for Ford Motor Co. and the United Auto Workers broke off talks for the night to get some rest on Sunday after failing to reach agreement on a new national labor contract.
The negotiations were expected to resume on Monday at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT) and production at Ford's U.S. plants was expected to proceed without disruption, the automaker said.
UAW officials said the two sides were still at odds over key economic, job and parts subcontracting issues that will affect Ford's 105,000 hourly UAW workers.
"Nothing is settled until you get the whole agreement," said Carl Dowell, president of UAW Local 862 at Ford's Louisville, Ky., truck plants.
Ford, however, tried to put a more positive spin on the recess. "I think things are proceeding well. People just need some rest," said Ford spokesman Jon Harmon.
In a statement, Ford said its negotiating teams "will return at eight in the morning and have agreed that they will continue at that time with the intention of reaching an agreement."
The company added that negotiators "have worked steadily and effectively almost the entire weekend, including through Saturday night".

Ford and UAW sources also confirmed on Sunday that they reached a tentative agreement covering about 750 salaried workers represented by the union, including designers and product development employees. Details of that agreement were not immediately available.

In the pact affecting hourly workers, the union has sought to guarantee minimum employment levels and provisions that restrict the company's ability to shift work to outside suppliers, including establishing the right to strike over such decisions.
According to some published reports on Sunday, Ford and the UAW were prepared to agree to minimum employment levels below the 105,000 current employees.
Dowell said that would be tough to sell to the membership, which wants to increase jobs.
"You need to say, 'We're going to keep all our jobs, and we're going to grow,'" he said. "The best contract in the world doesn't mean a thing if you haven't got a job."
Although the union did not formally extend the Ford contract, it urged workers to report to work as normal.
A number of Ford parts plants were operating normally on Sunday, but production of cars and trucks at Ford's 15 U.S. assembly plants were not scheduled to resume until Monday morning.
At UAW local halls around the country, union officials awaited word of a settlement but remained prepared to strike.
"People are getting pretty anxious," said John Kimbro, president of UAW Local 737 at Ford's glass plant in Nashville, Tenn. "Nobody really wants to go out on strike."
With only a four-hour break early Sunday, about 400 people negotiating the pact met for about 33 hours on Saturday and Sunday.
The weekend's activity ended early optimism that a deal would be reached with unprecedented swiftness.

Dale Brickner, associate director of Michigan State University's labor relations department, said on Sunday that more negotiating time may have been needed to make sure the UAW can also sell the pattern contract to General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp..
"They may be going slower to make sure that everybody's on board when they reach an agreement," Brickner said.
The UAW, with nearly 400,000 workers at all three companies, extended contracts at GM and Chrysler while it concentrated on Ford.
Negotiations between the UAW and the "Big Three" ran past contract expiration deadlines in each of the past three pacts -- 1987, 1990 and 1993.
